doc.title: Tony Marino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 25, 2025

title: Scott LaFaro and the soloistic bass
summary: Marino explains LaFaro's role in Bill Evans's trio and how bassists imitating him upset bandleaders.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Okay you have to explain that.

Well okay, Scott LaFaro was a heavy member of Bill Evans’ trio. Piano trio. And Bill had a new concept which was the bass part doesn’t hold the time-keeping role, which you mentioned before. He’s more of a counterpoint player you know. And more of a soloist. And Scott was a genius you know. Also a heavy practitioner. He practiced a lot. So he was able to do horn-like riffs on the bass and we marveled at his virtuosity. You know. And stories I’ve heard, I wasn’t there you know, I never got to see him play live, but stories I heard was when Bill Evans’ trio played live there was a long line of bass players going in to hear him play. And they were all crazy. So when they got on their gigs whether it was a dance gig or whatever, they tried to imitate him and the band leaders were going nuts because they weren’t playing time. They weren’t playing the dance music.
Yeah. You know they all wanted to solo and play in the upper register you know? So the bottom of the band would drop out. We couldn’t wait for our moment you know.
I think that kind of influence has even gone into the current day where, especially with electric bass players.
You know they have the facility to play like a saxophone player and so they’re going to.

I equate it more to guitar you know. ‘Cause it’s a whole different feel, horizontally playing. And these guys, I mean electric bass players and guitar players, you know, really get along. But you know, definitely horn players. Yeah.
